transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-22
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Sanjay Rao (Atlas Eng Mgr), Maya Ortiz (Atlas SRE), Liam Chen (Atlas Security), Aisha Khan (Atlas Product)

Summary:
Quick console walkthrough focused on tracing, error analysis and request logs. Customer is evaluating Redwood for a pilot to replace current hosted endpoints; main concerns: latency SLOs for critical pathways, observability for request failure modes, and security/compliance (SAML, KMS, audit logs, data residency). Agreed next steps: share SOC2/compliance pack, schedule benchmark run with sample traffic, and surface dedicated pricing.

Topics:
- Tracing UI and linking traces to request logs
- Error analysis workflow (root-cause, correlation with models/versions)
- Request logs exploration: filters, payload redaction, retention policies
- Security controls: audit logs, KMS, SSO/SAML, VPC access
- Pilot and benchmark plan

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, this is Jordan from Redwood. Uh, we'll do, a quick walkthrough of the console today, focusing on tracing and request logs. Priya will take most of the demo.
[00:07] Priya: Hi team, yeah hi, thanks. So first thing I'll share my screen — lemme know if you can't see it.
[00:13] Maya: We can see it, looks good.
[00:15] Priya: Great. So this is the Redwood Console, top left you can see the service selector, we're scoped to the atlas-health-prod workspace for demo. Down here is the tracing tab. The traces are sampled at 10% in this view; you can adjust sampling and set deterministic sampling for canaries.
[00:33] Priya: I'll click into a trace — this one shows a high tail latency event on a text-generation route. The timeline on the right shows token-level breaks, and you can see a slow kernel selection step at around 250ms, and then a regen loop because of a function call back-off.
[00:47] Sanjay: Sorry, quick q — when you say kernel selection are you meaning the runtime picks a different quantized kernel based on sequence length?
[00:52] Priya: Yeah exactly — the runtime will pick a kernel path based on seq length heuristics and quantization profile. In some cases we see a cold-path where the model's kv cache wasn't primed and that adds overhead.
[01:02] Liam: Is that visible per-customer? Like, can we see which requests hit the cold-path vs warmed cache?
[01:07] Priya: Yep, we surface a 'cache-hit' tag on traces, you can filter traces by that. You can also link a trace to request logs to inspect input/output tokens and any attached metadata.
[01:15] Jordan: Also worth mentioning, you can export traces in JSON to import into third-party APMs, or keep them in Redwood for longer retention if you opt into extended retention add-on.
[01:24] Maya: What's the retention by default? We're sensitive about PII so need a short default.
[01:28] Priya: Default is 30 days for request logs and 7 days for traces in hosted tiers; dedicated or enterprise can configure retention and use your KMS for log encryption.
[01:37] Aisha: When you say use our KMS, do we have to be on private deployment? Or is that available on Dedicated?
[01:42] Priya: Good question. KMS integration (customer-managed keys) is supported on Dedicated and Private deployments. Hosted has envelope encryption with Redwood-managed keys today.
[01:51] Sanjay: Can you show the error analysis flow? We want to tie errors back to model version/route and alert on regressions.
[01:57] Priya: For sure. I'll go to Error Analysis — here the console aggregates error types (runtime errors, timeouts, model misalignments). You can group by model version, route, or prompt family. We also automatically surface regressions against baseline evals if you've uploaded eval sets.
[02:12] Priya: Let's pivot to a sample failure — here's a cluster of timeout errors on /generate-chat. Clicking one shows all requests for that window, with a link to stack trace and to the originating trace. You can jump straight to the offending token generation step, and also see correlated metrics — CPU/GPU utilization, queue length.
[02:30] Maya: That correlation view is great — can we create alert rules from it?
[02:34] Priya: Yes, you can create alerts from the analysis page (thresholds, rate-of-change), and tie them to notification channels or to automatic fallbacks (we can reroute to a smaller model or older pinned version until the problem is mitigated).
[02:46] Liam: About fallbacks, does the fallback preserve SLA? Like, switching to a smaller model reduces cost but latency still needs to meet our 200ms SLO for that endpoint.
[02:55] Jordan: We typically configure fallback policies with prioritized model list and per-model latency profiles. For strict latency SLOs we recommend Dedicated with pinned capacity so you have predictable tail latency.
[03:05] Sanjay: Can the console show per-token latency distribution? We want to see where in the token stream latency spikes happen.
[03:10] Priya: Yup — token-level histograms in traces. Here's a heatmap that shows token position vs p50/p95 latency; you can filter by route or by model quantization.
[03:21] [Small crosstalk]
[03:25] Priya: Now request logs. This is the request explorer — it has live tailing, queryable filters (route, model, status, user_id), and payload redaction rules.
[03:34] Priya: Notice the redaction column — we automatically mask user-defined PII fields and you can supply regex rules to scrub additional fields. Logs are searchable but payloads are encrypted at rest.
[03:45] Aisha: Can logs be forwarded to our Splunk/Datadog?
[03:48] Priya: Yes, we have log forwarders; you can stream request metadata (and optionally full payloads if permitted) to your SIEM via HTTPS or to S3, and we support structured JSON export.
[03:58] Sanjay: About sampling — would streaming full payloads of all requests be viable for a high-traffic endpoint? That's a lot of egress and cost.
[04:04] Priya: Right, which is why we support conditional sampling: capture 100% of errors + 1% of success requests, or capture by user segment. That reduces egress but keeps visibility into failure modes.
[04:14] Liam: On compliance, audit logs — are admin actions (deploys, rollouts, KMS config changes) captured?
[04:19] Priya: Yes, audit logs capture admin activity and are immutable; you can push them to your SIEM and we also surface them in the console for admins.
[04:26] Jordan: Quick note on SSO — we support SAML and SCIM for provisioning, plus role-based access control to limit who can view traces or decrypt payloads.
[04:35] Maya: Do you mask prompts in the console UI for non-privileged roles?
[04:39] Priya: Yes, view permissions control whether you can see raw prompts or only metadata; only users with 'logs:read' and 'secrets:decrypt' roles (or equivalent) can view decrypted payloads.
[04:48] Sanjay: Ok, let's talk pilot — we'll want to baseline: latency p95, cost per 1k tokens, and error rates across our top 3 routes.
[04:57] Jordan: Totally. Action items — Jordan will send pricing/pilot agreement; Priya will run a benchmark with your sample traffic and share the runbook. We recommend running both 1) synthetic p95 stress and 2) replay of a 24h sample to catch cache-warmup behavior.
[05:15] Aisha: One more quick thing — do you support dedicated VPC peering for Dedicated deployments?
[05:20] Priya: Yes, Dedicated supports VPC peering and Private (on-prem) supports air-gapped installs. Dedicated gives you customer-managed KMS, private networking and audit capabilities without the full private control plane.
[05:30] Liam: For the benchmark, we need to know what telemetry you will collect; will you send us a summary report with token-level latencies and a CSV of traces?
[05:37] Priya: We'll provide a benchmarking report with p50/p95/p99, token-level histogram samples, sample trace JSONs and an issue log if regressions are detected.
[05:46] Jordan: Cool — any other Qs?
[05:50] Maya: Nothing from me.
[05:52] Sanjay: Nope.
[05:53] Aisha: All good.
[05:54] Jordan: Ok we'll follow up with the docs and the pilot agreement. Thanks everybody.
